lines.text: Seasonings and condiments transform plain food into flavourful meals. Seasonings are added during cooking to enhance flavour. The most basic are salt and pepper — found on every dining table and in every kitchen. Herbs are the leaves of aromatic plants: basil, oregano, thyme, rosemary, parsley, coriander (cilantro), and mint each bring distinct flavours. Spices come from seeds, bark, roots, and fruits: cumin, cinnamon, turmeric, paprika, chilli powder, and nutmeg add depth and warmth. Garlic and ginger, though technically vegetables, function as essential seasonings. Condiments are prepared sauces and accompaniments served alongside food. Ketchup, mustard, and mayonnaise are the classic trio for sandwiches and burgers. Soy sauce, fish sauce, and oyster sauce are staples in Asian cooking. Vinegar, olive oil, and lemon juice form the base of most salad dressings. Hot sauce and chilli paste add heat for those who enjoy spicy food. Relishes, chutneys, and pickles offer tangy, sweet, or savoury accompaniments. Understanding the distinction between seasonings (added during cooking) and condiments (served at the table) is important. A well-stocked pantry with a variety of seasonings and condiments empowers any cook to create diverse, flavourful dishes from around the world.

lines.text: British English uses 'coriander' for both the leaf and the seed. American English uses 'cilantro' for the leaf and 'coriander' for the seed. This is one of the most confusing UK/US food vocabulary differences.

lines.text: Britain has a strong condiment culture: HP Sauce (brown sauce), Branston Pickle, Marmite, English mustard, mint sauce (for lamb), and horseradish sauce (for beef). Knowing these helps understand British food culture and restaurant menus.

lines.text: Many English spice words come from Arabic, Hindi, and Malay — reflecting centuries of spice trade. 'Cumin' (Arabic: kamun), 'turmeric' (Latin/Arabic), 'ginger' (Sanskrit), 'saffron' (Arabic: za'faran). This linguistic heritage enriches English vocabulary.

lines.text: Hot sauce has its own vocabulary: 'Scoville scale' measures heat, 'ghost pepper' and 'Carolina Reaper' are extremely hot varieties. In the UK, 'Nando's' popularised 'peri-peri' sauce. Americans love 'Tabasco' and 'Sriracha'.

lines.text: English distinguishes between 'fresh herbs' (living/recently cut) and 'dried herbs' (dehydrated). Recipes specify which to use because flavour intensity differs. A common rule: use 1/3 the amount of dried herbs compared to fresh.
